summary: Return the k-th smallest element of an n x n matrix whose rows and columns are sorted, using less than O(n^2) memory.
mainInsight: Binary search on the value, not the index: for a candidate x, count elements <= x with a staircase walk from the bottom-left corner in O(n). The smallest x with count >= k is the answer, and it is always an element of the matrix.
invariant: lo <= answer <= hi throughout; count(<= hi) >= k and count(<= lo - 1) < k.
canonicalApproach: Binary search on value with staircase counting

approaches.name: Flatten and sort
approaches.summary: Copy all n^2 values and sort.

approaches.name: Max-heap of size k over all cells
approaches.summary: Push every value, pop when size exceeds k.

approaches.name: Min-heap of row heads (k-way merge)
approaches.summary: Push the first of each row; pop k times, pushing the next in that row.

approaches.name: Binary search on value with staircase counting
approaches.summary: Binary search x in [matrix[0][0], matrix[-1][-1]], count <= x in O(n).

personalSolution.approach: Max-heap of size k over all n^2 cells
personalSolution.spaceComplexity: O(k), which is O(n^2) when k is close to n^2
personalSolution.notes: Correct, but it ignores that rows and columns are sorted, and its memory reaches O(n^2) for large k, which the statement rules out. Use a min-heap of row heads (O(n) memory) or binary search on the value with a staircase count (O(1) memory).

commonMistakes: Binary searching on positions, which are not globally sorted.
Using count == k as the stop condition (duplicates make it skip).
Returning mid instead of converging to lo.
A heap over all n^2 cells, which violates the memory requirement.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Binary search on the value range, counting elements <= mid with a staircase walk. Clue: Every row and column is sorted and the memory must be better than storing the whole matrix, so you can count how many elements are at most x without listing them.
keyPoints: Every row and column is sorted and the memory must be better than storing the whole matrix, so you can count how many elements are at most x without listing them.
cards.explanation: 'k-th smallest' plus a cheap 'how many are <= x' count is binary search on the answer; the sorted rows also allow a k-way heap merge.

aliases: k-way merge of the rows with a heap

promptVariants: Why is the binary search on values rather than on indices?
What makes count(<= x) usable for binary search?
options: count(<= x) never decreases as x grows
The flattened matrix is sorted row by row
The diagonal of the matrix is strictly increasing
Every value appears at most once
cards.answer: count(<= x) never decreases as x grows
cards.explanation: The yes/no question 'are at least k elements <= x' flips from no to yes exactly once, so the first yes is the k-th smallest value.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The flattened matrix is sorted row by ro: matrix[0][-1] can be larger than matrix[1][0].
incorrectOptionExplanations.The diagonal of the matrix is strictly i: Only non-decreasing, and it does not give a global order.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Every value appears at most once: Duplicates are allowed; the note says k-th smallest, not k-th distinct.

promptVariants: In the staircase count from the bottom-left, what happens when matrix[r][c] <= x?
How does count_le advance when the current cell is <= x?
options: Add n - r and move right
cards.explanation: Columns are sorted, so every cell above (r, c) in column c is <= x too: r + 1 cells. Then the next column may have more.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Add 1 and move up: That counts one cell at a time and loses the column shortcut.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Add c + 1 and move up: That would count a row prefix, but we are standing at the bottom of a column.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Add n - r and move right: That counts the cells below, which are larger.

promptVariants: For [[1, 2], [1, 3]] and k = 2, what is the k-th smallest?
cards.explanation: Sorted values are 1, 1, 2, 3; duplicates count separately, so the 2nd smallest is 1. count_le(1) = 2 >= k, so the search stops at 1.

incorrectOptionExplanations.2: That is the 2nd distinct value; duplicates count.
incorrectOptionExplanations.1.5: The answer is always an element of the matrix; integer mid avoids fractions.

promptVariants: Your solution keeps a max-heap of size k over every cell. What is its cost, and why does it miss the memory requirement?
Critique this heap solution against the constraints.
cards.answer: It pushes all n^2 cells with O(log k) each, so O(n^2 log k) time, and the heap holds k values. k can be up to n^2, so memory can reach O(n^2), which the statement forbids. It also never uses the sorted rows and columns. A min-heap of row heads keeps memory O(n); binary search on the value with a staircase count uses O(1).
keyPoints: Heap size k, up to n^2
cards.explanation: Generic top-k is a fine first answer, but here the constraint explicitly asks for something better.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code? (D = max - min value)
Derive the running time of binary search with staircase counting.
cards.explanation: The value range halves each step: O(log D) iterations, each with an O(n) staircase walk (at most 2n moves).

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^2 log D): Counting by scanning every cell, not the staircase.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n): The search is over values, so it depends on the value range.

promptVariants: The binary search with staircase counting uses O(___) extra space.
Extra space of the canonical code: O(___).
cards.explanation: Only lo, hi, mid and the walk indices; this easily meets the better-than-O(n^2) requirement.
